column4: The section reads Iram’s height and its dictionary memory of Iram as a desert marker together. Hud’s question about placing a sign on every high place for play gives that raised-marker image a specific Qur’anic scene.
The section says Ad’s structures look as though their builders expect to live forever. Hud’s next question names their constructed works and that very presumption of lasting life.

The section quotes Ad’s claim of unmatched strength. This ayah gives the voice behind construction on high places and works assumed to last, making the monuments an expression of their own confidence.
The section describes Pharaoh ordering mud fired and a tower made so he can ascend toward Moses’ God. This ayah stages that precise construction and intention in Pharaoh’s own command.

The section’s Pharaoh tries to build a tower to reach upward. This later account has Pharaoh tell Haman to build a tower; the next ayah, 40:37, specifies the hoped-for ascent through the ways of heaven.
The section links Pharaoh’s tower to his attempt to reach Moses’ God. This neighboring ayah supplies the intended ascent through heavenly ways and Pharaoh’s judgment that Moses is a liar.

The section explains Pharaoh’s title as possessor of stakes, driven into earth to hold something in place. This ayah names Pharaoh with that title among earlier rejecters, placing the title in a history of defying messengers.

The section says transgression is going above a boundary and names Pharaoh’s overreach. This ayah says Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people, giving that upward domination its political form.

The section’s dictionary branch for ط غ ي explains transgression as rising beyond a limit and applies it to Pharaoh. Here Moses is sent to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, the section’s vertical sense stated as a command’s reason.
The section reads Pharaoh’s height as overstepping a boundary. Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest lord turns that image into an explicit claim to supreme authority.
The section connects transgression with overstepping and pairs Pharaoh’s rise with human overreach. This ayah uses the named root for the human who transgresses.

The section identifies seeing oneself as beyond need as the condition for human transgression. This neighboring ayah states that cause, linking the image to self-sufficiency that lets a person imagine limits do not apply.

The section calls Hicr the home of Thamud and says its people denied the messengers. This ayah identifies the people of al-Hijr as rejecters of messengers, grounding the rock-dwelling scene in its own context.
The section describes Thamud cutting homes into the hardest rock and says they felt secure there. This ayah gives the exact mountain-carved, secure-house scene.

The section says the secure rock dwellings did not protect Thamud from an end arriving in the morning. This neighboring ayah names the cry that seized them at morning; 15:82 supplies the houses, while this row supplies their sudden end.
The section’s Semud image is people cutting houses into rock. Salih’s speech here says they carved homes from mountains and built palaces in the plain, joining mountain-work to settlement.
The section emphasizes the skill and force needed to open hard rock. Salih’s warning here names their skillful carving of houses from mountains, a direct formulation of that craft.
The section defines Pharaoh’s stakes as supports driven into the ground. This ayah calls the mountains pegs, giving the same support image to God’s ordering of the earth.

The section treats pegs as supports that steady what is above them. This ayah says firm mountains were placed in the earth so it would not shake and mentions passes as roads, assigning stability and passage to God’s world.

The section defines د ك ك as breaking a wall or mountain until it is level with the earth. In Moses’ encounter, the mountain is made dakk and Moses falls unconscious, a direct mountain-crushing scene.

The section says even a built height will be flattened when God’s promise arrives. Dhul-Qarnayn says his barrier is a mercy for now and that his Lord will make it level when the promise comes, a constructed defense with a divinely set end.

The section describes the earth being struck flat and says mountains lose their separate height. This ayah brings earth and mountains together under one crushing blow, the broad judgment scene behind that image.
The section cites the land left as a level plain after the mountains are removed. This ayah gives that flat expanse, tying the section’s dekk image to the mountain-removal scene.
The section cites a surface with neither hollow nor rise. This ayah specifies no crookedness or elevation on the plain, so the distinction between standing heights and low ground disappears.

The section describes mountains and human works losing their height. This neighboring judgment scene removes the mountains, leaves the earth exposed, and gathers everyone; 18:48 then places them in a row.

The section’s 89:22 image has the Lord arrive with angels in ranks on the flattened ground. Here people are presented to their Lord in a row after the mountains have been removed in 18:47, joining leveling to ordered assembly.
The section links the flat plain with the ranks of the final gathering. This ayah says the Spirit and angels stand in a row on that Day, a direct parallel to the ordered heavenly presence.

The section contrasts being forced low with the chosen lowliness of a gentle walk and explicitly cites this root use. Here the servants of the Merciful walk on earth humbly, a positive, voluntary counterpart to fallen monuments.

The section says Iram’s raised columns need physical support and that human height fails when its column falls. This ayah says Allah raised the heavens without columns visible to people, shifting the same vertical image from dependent construction to divine power.

The section says human height depends on supports while Allah’s height does not. This ayah repeats the heavens-without-visible-pillars image and pairs it with mountains set in the earth, a direct boundary on human claims to structural mastery.

The section treats rising beyond a limit as arrogance. This ayah forbids arrogant walking and says a person cannot split the earth or reach the mountains in height, making the boundary of human ascent concrete.
The section sets human overreach against voluntary humility. This ayah forbids contemptuous turning and walking the earth exultantly, naming the posture that the section’s low, gentle gait reverses.

The section says Thamud ended prostrate in their dwelling places after cutting secure homes from rock. This ayah places them in their homes, brought low after their rebellion; the built refuge has become the setting of their collapse.

The section says Ad’s tall bodies end as hollow palm trunks lying on the ground. This ayah gives that exact image after the destructive wind, turning the people who boasted of strength into fallen trunks.

The section reads Ad’s hollow palm trunks as upright forms brought down. This parallel says the wind tore them out like uprooted palm trunks, making the reversal from height to fallen bodies explicit.

The section’s Thamud houses are followed by people brought low in their home. This neighboring account says it was as if they had never lived there, connecting collapse to the erased trace named by the section’s dictionary branch.

The section’s م ث ل discussion holds a standing form and a form leveled to earth in one word. This account of earlier towns says some are still standing and some have been cut down, giving that opposed posture as a history of settlements.

The section describes Pharaoh’s tower and stakes among human works that cannot endure. This ayah says God destroyed what Pharaoh and his people made and erected, giving the physical reversal of that architecture.

The section labels ع م د as a support or pillar carrying a load. This ayah uses the same root for extended columns in the scene of the sealed fire: columns no longer support a monument but belong to confinement.

The section says Iram has no likeness among the lands and traces the claim through م ث ل. This ayah uses the same comparison-root to say nothing is like God, setting a finite city’s uniqueness against the ultimate limit on likeness.

The section questions the claim that reduced provision means God has humiliated someone and shows rulers’ height ending. This prayer says God gives and removes sovereignty and honors or abases whom He wills, placing worldly rank under His authority.

The section moves from raised structures to forced lowering and says no human height persists. This ayah places the sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, creatures, and many people in prostration, then says the one God humiliates has no one to honor him.

The section’s Pharaoh orders a tower to reach Moses’ God and treats worldly power as lasting. At the close of that narrative, this ayah says everything perishes except God, giving a direct limit to the permanence the tower claims.
The section levels the monuments and dwellings that seemed fixed in the earth. This ayah states that those on earth pass away, extending the leveling image from structures to their makers.
The section cites Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest lord. This preceding ayah says he gathered his people and called out, supplying the public setting for the boast stated in 79:24.

The section sets Ad’s boast of unmatched power beside works that cannot stand. This neighboring ayah describes a humiliating wind sent after the boast in 41:15, showing that claimed strength did not protect them.

The section portrays Pharaoh’s height and structures as displays of worldly power. Pharaoh here points to Egypt’s kingdom and rivers as proof of his greatness, making the landscape itself part of his boast.

The section shows Pharaoh’s overreach joined to judging others as low. In the next ayah he calls Moses contemptible and barely articulate; that status judgment contrasts his own claim to height and power.
The section says the mountain-cut houses felt secure but could not save their makers. This ayah immediately adds that what they had earned did not avail them, making the failure of security explicit.
The section gives Thamud’s rock-built security and their prostrate end. This preceding ayah supplies their defiance and killing of the she-camel; 7:78 gives the collapse that follows.

The section pairs Thamud’s carved settlement with their end in their dwellings. This parallel account says the cry seized the wrongdoers and left them prostrate in their homes; 11:68 then says it was as if they had never lived there.

The section names Thamud among those who transgressed and explains ط غ ي as going beyond a limit. This ayah says Thamud denied in their transgression, a direct application of the same moral frame to the rock-carving people.
The section links Thamud’s transgression with overstepping a limit. This next ayah identifies the most wretched one as the one who rose up, specifying the agent within 91:11’s transgression.

The section pairs Thamud’s skill in cutting enormous rock with their destruction. This account says a single cry left them like dry broken stalks, reversing the strength of carved stone into brittle remains.

The section names Thamud for carving hard rock and ends with their collapse in their dwellings. This ayah gives their destruction by the overwhelming blast, the force that undoes the apparent security of their stone homes.

The section connects Ad’s end with bodies fallen like palm trunks. This neighboring ayah names the violent, continuous wind that leads into the trunk image in 54:20; it supplies the force behind the fall.

The section describes Ad’s people as fallen palm trunks. This neighboring ayah names the furious wind that precedes that image in 69:7, giving the means by which their apparent strength was overturned.

The section calls attention to a city’s erased trace and to built height brought level with the ground. This neighboring ayah asks whether any remnant of Ad can be seen after the fallen-trunk image in 69:7, supplying the question of what remains.

The section’s distinctive mountain settlement ends as a place without its people. This ayah points to Thamud’s houses left empty because of their wrongdoing, joining the carved dwellings to the trace of a vanished community.

The section groups Ad and Thamud through their built works and their end. This ayah mentions both nations and says their dwellings became clear after them, adding the physical remainder to the narrative of their destruction.

The section says Ad’s extraordinary built presence does not keep its height. This ayah describes a wind destroying everything by its Lord’s command, leaving only their dwellings visible, a specific aftermath for Ad.

The section takes Iram as a singular city whose makers could not preserve its height. This ayah recalls many destroyed prosperous towns whose dwellings were not inhabited after them, making abandoned architecture the remainder of worldly power.

The section’s dictionary memory calls Iram a desert marker and presents Pharaoh as a ruler who sought to rise toward heaven. This ayah says Pharaoh’s body was preserved as a sign for later people, making the fallen ruler a marker after his failed rebellion.

The section relates cities’ destruction to the peoples’ overreach. This neighboring ayah says the towns were not wronged but wronged themselves, completing 11:100’s standing and cut-down settlements with the cause of their fall.

The section sets human stakes against supports God places in the world and recalls Iram as a desert marker. This ayah describes mountains set firm, roads, and guidance, a related scene of fixed orientation without naming marker stones.

The section’s labeled memory for Iram is a stone set as a landmark in open country. This ayah names landmarks and star-guidance, supporting the wayfinding function though it does not say the landmarks are stones.

The section’s dictionary branch for ج و ب compares cutting a hard-rock opening to making a garment’s neck opening. In Moses’ encounter with Pharaoh, this ayah puts his hand into his garment opening, supplying the soft-material aperture used by the section’s comparison.

The section’s named خ ل ق branch means bringing something forth without a prior model. This ayah calls God the Originator of the heavens and earth and says He created all things, placing Iram’s claimed novelty beside a Creator’s making.

The section contrasts a plain smashed level from a road made smooth by being walked. This ayah describes the earth spread out like a carpet, establishing the surface across which the next ayah’s paths run.
The section describes a road made smooth through use. This neighboring ayah says paths are made across the spread earth for people to travel, giving the traveled surface a concrete counterpart.

The section cites the answer that mountains become a level plain. This preceding ayah asks about the mountains and introduces the response in 20:106–107; its contribution is the question that frames their removal.

The section distinguishes ground smashed flat from a path made smooth by walking and speaks of entering among God’s servants. This next ayah says people follow the caller without deviation and voices are humbled, linking the level plain to a directed, humbled response.

The section connects صَفّ to a flat line and to the ordered gathering. This ayah opens with those arrayed in ranks, a direct example of the same root in an ordered row rather than as a description of earth.

The section reads صفّ as a straight line across a level plain. This ayah says the servants stand in ranks and then glorify God, giving the row a worshipful order rather than the fame-seeking monument.

The section’s monuments stand apart and are later flattened. This ayah praises those who stand in rank in God’s cause like a compact structure, a collective structure whose alignment rather than private height is commended.

The section’s dictionary branch for ع ب د calls a well-used road a smoothed, trodden way and reads the invitation among God’s servants beside it. This ayah names a straight path to God, making the path-and-servant association explicit.

The section connects entry among God’s servants with a trodden-road image. This next ayah names God’s servants and says Satan has no authority over them except followers who go astray, completing the straight-path statement in 15:41.
The section leaves human buildings level with the earth. This adjacent ayah says the Lord of majesty and honor remains, completing 55:26’s passing away with what endures.

The section says no human support can preserve a raised monument. This ayah depicts the whole earth in God’s grasp and the heavens rolled up on Resurrection Day, giving the final scale of divine mastery over the built world.

The section’s craft reading of خ ل ق includes measuring material before cutting. This ayah pairs creation with precise determination, giving a related measure-and-making formulation, though its root is not the source’s craft verb.

The section’s dictionary branch for خ ل ق includes measuring leather before cutting. This ayah says created things are made according to measure; the link is a secondary root reading, not the verse’s claim about Iram.

The section’s dictionary branch for مُطْمَئِنَّة carries a low, settled contour. This ayah uses the same root for hearts finding rest in God’s remembrance; treating inner rest as the image’s low ground is an uncertain extension.

The section says the root ط غ ي first carries the sense of water exceeding its bounds and also names a high place. This ayah recalls the flood’s water overflowing its limit, directly supplying the physical rise behind that dictionary connection.

The section’s dictionary branch for ط غ ي treats transgression as rising beyond a limit and applies it to Pharaoh. This ayah gives Moses the command to confront Pharaoh because he has transgressed, a repeated formulation in Pharaoh’s story.
The section names Pharaoh among those who cross their bounds. Here Moses and Aaron are jointly sent to Pharaoh for the same stated reason, repeating the transgression that motivates the mission.
The section cites Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest lord. This next ayah says God seized him with punishment in this life and the next, supplying the reversal immediately after the boast in 79:24.
The section turns Pharaoh’s visible height into a warning about overreach. This neighboring ayah says his seizure is a lesson for one who fears, giving the intended response to that example.

The section compares Pharaoh’s tower and Iram’s columns with God’s raising of the heavens without visible supports. This ayah asks whether human creation or the heaven is harder, then names God as its builder.
The section sets human-built height against God’s own raised heaven. This ayah says its ceiling was raised and proportioned, a divine height that bounds Pharaoh’s attempt to ascend by construction.

The section contrasts human stakes with supports established by God. In the same creation passage as 79:27–28, this ayah says God set the mountains firmly, repeating the natural peg image in the section.

The section defines transgression as going above bounds and later contrasts forced lowering with chosen humility. This ayah names the person who transgresses, carrying the same root into the judgment between those two paths.

The section distinguishes being forcibly brought down from willingly taking a lowly path. This ayah describes the person who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire, the chosen restraint opposite transgression.

The section pairs the people of Hicr’s rejection of messengers with their confidence in rock-carved homes. This intervening ayah says they were given signs but turned away, showing that their material security accompanied refusal of guidance.

The section cites Dhul-Qarnayn’s barrier as a built work that God will eventually flatten. This preceding ayah introduces the barrier between the mountains and Dhul-Qarnayn’s offer to build it with the people’s help.

The section says even a formidable wall has a divinely set end. This ayah details the iron and molten-copper construction of Dhul-Qarnayn’s barrier; 18:97 then says the people could neither climb nor pierce it.

The section contrasts tall structures with the earth made level at God’s appointed time. This ayah says Gog and Magog cannot climb or pierce the completed barrier, making its present strength specific before 18:98 names its eventual leveling.

The section says Thamud felt secure in mountain-carved houses. This ayah describes people who thought their fortresses would protect them, yet were expelled from their homes; it gives a direct reversal of confidence in built defense.
The section connects the ground leveled by God with mountains described as pegs. This preceding ayah calls the earth a resting place, completing the earth-and-mountain pair that 78:7 supplies.

The section groups Ad’s high-place monuments with transgression. In Hud’s same speech, this ayah says they seize others like tyrants, giving their architectural overreach a concrete form of domination.

The section moves from Ad’s constructions and claim to lasting power toward their disappearance. This concluding ayah in Hud’s account says they denied him and were destroyed, supplying the fate after 26:128–130.

The section treats mountains and stone structures as heights that can be brought down. This ayah says mountains that appear fixed will pass like clouds on the Day of Judgment, overturning the appearance of permanence.

The section’s dictionary branch for خ ل ق includes a trace leveled to earth, and it follows towns whose traces disappear. This ayah asks who will revive bones after they have decayed, making erased remains the subject of a resurrection challenge.

The section links the erased trace to the root خ ل ق and the Day of leveling. This answer says the One who created the bones the first time will revive them, completing 36:78 with creation after decay.

The section contrasts ground flattened by force with a road made smooth by being walked, then calls the soul into God’s servants. This ayah says to follow God’s straight path and not diverging paths, making the chosen route a concrete moral counterpart.

The section contrasts the flattened earth with the road made traversable through use. In Moses’ exchange with Pharaoh, this ayah says God made the earth a resting place and its paths for travel, grounding the path image in God’s creation.

The section distinguishes a crushed plain from a path made smooth by passage. This ayah joins the earth as a resting place with roads laid through it, a repeated formulation of the surface-and-route image.

The section describes the present earth and mountains losing their distinct heights at judgment. This ayah says the earth will be changed for another earth and the heavens as all come before God, another specific formulation of that transformed scene.

The section compares human towers with the heaven raised by God without visible columns. This ayah asks its hearer to look at the sky and how it was raised, repeating the vertical image as a sign of divine making.
The section describes mountains as supports and as heights later leveled. This ayah asks how the mountains were set up, placing their established height among signs of the Creator.
The section’s final scene leaves the earth level after mountains are removed. This ayah asks how the earth was spread out, giving a creation-side counterpart to the judgment plain.

The section contrasts God’s crushing of the earth with humanly smoothed paths. This ayah says the earth was spread after the heaven was raised, completing the same vertical-and-grounded landscape in creation.

The section treats raised works as a way of claiming lasting life. This neighboring ayah says the transgressor preferred the nearer life, specifying the worldly preference behind the upward display named in 79:37.
The section shows high structures brought low at judgment. This neighboring ayah names Hell as the transgressor’s destination, giving the consequence of the worldly path in 79:37–38.

The section’s final image calls a soul into God’s servants and toward the Garden. This neighboring ayah names the Garden as the home of the person who restrains the self in 79:40, completing the chosen path opposite transgression.

The section pairs Thamud’s impressive works with an account of human height and lowliness. This ayah contrasts the arrogant chiefs with those regarded as weak, showing status division among the same people who carved the mountain homes.

The section presents Thamud’s construction alongside their transgression. This ayah says the arrogant ones rejected what Salih’s followers believed, making the community’s haughtiness explicit before the camel incident in 7:77.

The section describes raised structures and mountains later leveled. This ayah recalls a mountain raised above the Israelites when they took a covenant, a divine height held over people rather than built for human permanence.

The section makes human elevation answerable to God’s command. This ayah again places the mountain above the Israelites with the covenant and tells them to hold firmly to what was given, a repeated scene of imposed height and obligation.

The section describes mountains and structures whose height cannot last. This ayah recalls the mountain raised over the people for their covenant, another formulation in which a mountain’s position marks a boundary set by God.

The section contrasts the apparent security of rock-built homes with mountains brought low. This ayah depicts a mountain held above a people like a canopy as they fear its fall, making the same material a threat rather than shelter.

The section defines صَخْر as large, hard stone and pairs it with Thamud’s rejection of messengers. This ayah compares hardened hearts to stone, then says some stones split or fall in awe of God—a stone-centered counterimage to rejection.

The section calls Ad’s fallen people hollow palm trunks and describes the collapse of raised things. This ayah speaks of palm trees cut down or left standing by God’s permission, a specific reversal between what falls and what remains upright.
The section describes Pharaoh’s tower, stakes, and claims to supremacy. This ayah lists the fine stations his people left behind, making the loss of their worldly standing concrete.
The section says Pharaoh’s height and structures could not secure permanence. This neighboring ayah says those possessions were inherited by another people, specifying where the former power went.

The section presents Pharaoh among rulers brought down despite their height. This ayah says the heavens and earth did not grieve for them and they were not reprieved, an explicit image of their departure without lasting claim.

The section names a bent back as a secondary contour of the low, settled soul and contrasts voluntary humility with forced lowering. This ayah depicts believers bowing and prostrating, a bodily low posture; the posture link is specific, though the verse uses no root named by the section.

The section’s ج و ب dictionary example measures rock-cut openings by a garment’s neck opening. In Moses’ sign before Pharaoh, this ayah puts his hand into the garment opening, repeating the aperture detail in a second account.

The section defines transgression as exceeding a limit and names Thamud among the transgressors. This neighboring ayah records Salih’s warning that the she-camel has her allotted drink, stating the boundary that the next ayah’s people violate.
The section links Thamud’s transgression to their downfall. This next ayah says they denied Salih and hamstrung the she-camel, naming the concrete violation before the punishment summarized in 91:15.

The section’s dictionary entry for د ك ك uses a flat-backed, hump-less camel to explain levelness. This ayah asks the reader to consider how the camel was created, a specific animal echo, though it does not mention a missing hump or flat back.

The section’s dictionary branch for ع م د includes a tent pole. This ayah describes portable skin shelters alongside homes; it supplies a Qur’anic tent scene for that secondary sense, although it says nothing about poles.

The section links hard rock with works whose trace is erased. This ayah pictures a smooth stone with a thin covering left bare by rain, a specific image of exposed stone and vanished covering, though its own subject is failed charity.
